title: Amitabha
hookLine: Buddha of Infinite Light and Infinite Life
last: THE DOOR IS OPEN: TRUST AND THE NAME.

cards: A gilded figure seated on a temple altar in Japan, hands in the lap, fingers and thumbs forming two small circles.

A tall standing figure in a Chinese hall, one hand raised, the other lowered and open, as if reaching down to someone. A small paper image taped above a bed in a nursing home. Three images, one Buddha.
In Japan he's Amida. In China, Amituofo. In the Sanskrit sutras he carries two names, and today's word is the first: Amitabha.

teach.b: First, the two names, which the short sutra explains itself. You heard part of this with Honen; here's the whole. Why is that Buddha called Amitabha?
Because his light is measureless, shining without obstruction over the Buddha-lands in every direction. And why Amitayus? Because his life, and the life of the people in his land, is measureless too.
Amitabha, infinite light. Amitayus, infinite life. The Japanese Amida holds both.
Second, who he is: the monk from two days ago.
The longer sutra says Dharmakara kept his vows, became a Buddha, and lives now in the land of bliss. So every time someone says his name, they name a vow kept.
Sunlight on a city doesn't pick which roofs to land on, and in the sutra Amitabha's light reaches every land, near and far.
One clarification, since the shops confuse it: Amitabha isn't the laughing, round-bellied figure in gift shops. That's Budai, Hotei in Japan, a different figure altogether.

Fourth, how people meet him: through images like these, through the name in Japanese, Chinese, Korean and Vietnamese, and, the short sutra says, at the end of life, when he appears with a holy company before a dying person who has held his name in mind.
Some readers see that welcome in the standing statue's lowered hand.

how: Pure Land Buddhists keep images of Amitabha, seated or standing with one hand lowered in welcome, on temple and home altars, and call his name as Namu Amida Butsu in Japan or Namo Amituofo in China.

o: the laughing, round-bellied Buddha of gift shops
the Buddha of infinite light, Amida in Japan
the Buddha who taught Dharmakara long ago

s: Amitabha is the laughing, round-bellied Buddha
that's Budai, Hotei in Japan, a different figure altogether.
Amitabha and Amitayus are two names for the same Buddha
the short sutra explains both: measureless light and measureless life.
the sutra says his light reaches only the western lands
it shines without obstruction over the Buddha-lands in every direction.

games.q: you're Shariputra, and the Buddha asks you why that Buddha is called Amitabha. what's the sutra's answer?
o: because his land lies in the west.
because his light is measureless and shines without obstruction.
because he was once a king.
games.why: the short sutra gives the reason itself: measureless light, unobstructed in every direction. measureless life gives him his second name, Amitayus.

practice: Picture a small, warm light in the center of your chest, the size of a candle flame, and with each out-breath let it grow: your body, the room, the street, the city.
Let it spread until it has no edge and nothing blocks it, not walls, not distance, not anyone's past, and rest there, breathing.

wordCard.voice: Amitabha. The Buddha of infinite light, also called Amitayus, infinite life: Amida in Japan, Amituofo in China, the monk Dharmakara with his vows fulfilled. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Amitabha, infinite light. his second name, Amitayus (अमितायुस्), means infinite life. Japanese Amida (阿弥陀).

carryVoice: Your line: infinite light. A name that means a vow kept, shining in every direction. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Smaller Sukhavati-vyuha (why he is called Amitabha and Amitayus; his appearing at the end of life)
